items.title: The Theory of Contravariance, Part 2: Zippering
items.description: How end-to-end optimization strongly constrains upstream mechanisms and makes convergent evolution an inevitability... for minimal networks.
items.content:
(This is Part 2 of a series on Contravariance Theory. See Part 0 to get the big picture.)

Fig. 1: End-to-end optimization often gives rise to strong upstream constraints: e.g., optimizing for ImageNet categorization reliably yields a mixture of biologically recognizable monochrome Gabor wavelet and color-opponent center-surround filters, in an early V1-like layer.
Q: Why does this kind of thing happen?

One of the most striking observations in NeuroAI is that end-to-end optimization for downstream tasks often seems to strongly constrain upstream representations. And because (as we saw in Part 1 on Weak-Strong Equivalence) weak alignment of representations itself implies strong alignment of single-unit axes (assuming a hard enough task), this means that end-to-end optimization strongly constrains mechanism-level structures at a pretty fine-grained level. (And thus we find convergent evolution, as the Contravariance Principle claims; see Part 0.)

Thanks for reading The Principle Investigator! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

But why do we get strong upstream representational constraints in the first place? Nothing in the Weak-Strong Equivalence theorems implies this, since they start with the assumption of weak alignment in adjacent layers.

An Empirical “Zippering” Observation

Suppose you had a bunch of DNNs with the same architecture optimized for the same thing on the same dataset, but differing only in the random seed used at the start of training (so that weight initialization and training order differ). How would the representations of the different resulting fully trained networks compare?

Presumably the networks would be similar at the first layer (because they’re computed on the same images) and at the end, because they’re optimized for the same answers. But will the intermediate representations be highly constrained? Or will they “wander” far afield, finding mechanistically very different solutions away from the pinned-down first and last layers?

Here’s the answer we found in Thobani et al.:

Fig. 2: y-axis represents R^2 on held-out stimuli of ridge-regularized linear regressions between AlexNet architectures trained for ImageNet categorization from different seeds (error bars are SEM over 5 seeds). Dark green = post-nonlinearity; light green = pre-nonlinearity. (Reproduced from Thobani et al.).

Let’s focus first on the dark green bars, which represent comparisons after the nonlinearity at each layer — probably the most natural place to make the comparison from a neuroscience point of view.1 If you just looked at those layers, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the answer was “yes, lots of wandering happens”. Especially in intermediate layers 3 and 4, the representations are really quite different — even up to the “loose” weak-alignment standard of linear regression.

But now let’s look at the light green bars. These represent comparisons before the nonlinearity at each layer — that is, after the linear convolutional projection, but before ReLU. Now suddenly we see that the representations aren’t that different after all. Even intermediate layers are highly constrained to be similar. Somehow, what’s happening is that the resulting networks are quite close to being linearly aligned at each pre-nonlinearity layer. But then at each post-nonlinearity layer, the networks come apart. This alternation leads to a characteristic “zippering” (or “accordion”) pattern in which the networks’ representations repeatedly converge and diverge.

Apparently the system is not wandering that much after all. What’s going on?

With the Weak-Strong Equivalence theorems, we can interpret the post-nonlinearity divergence phenomenon: if the preactivation alignment is genuinely non-axis-preserving, and the used gates are used by the (presumably) hard task, then perfect post-ReLU linear alignment cannot (à la Part 1) persist. But we don’t see this: the next layer of affine operations, which are different for each seed, must suppress the seed-specific variability to cause re-convergence.

Of course, since invertible affine operations cannot reduce the dimension of a representation, the fact of re-convergence means that the affine operations are compressive. Specifically, the task-irrelevant dimensions have been pushed into seed-specific dimensions crossed by the used gates at the previous layer, and then are “squeezed out” by the re-convergent affine operations at the next layer. The empirical zippering observation is a visualization of the network iteratively focusing seed-independent common task-useful information into shared privileged axes at each layer.

Why does zippering happen in the first place?

BUT… what leads to the repeated re-convergence at each pre-nonlinearity layer in the first place? The Weak-Strong Equivalence mechanism does not answer this at all.

It turns out that there is a much stronger set of theorems, stated in section 4 of the Contravariance Theory paper, that explains this. The essential logic of the Weak-Strong Equivalence mechanism can be dramatically expanded to show that, under the right conditions, downstream weak equivalence induces weak equivalence at the previous layer; that equivalence, in turn, induces weak equivalence at the layer before it; and so on, “zippering” upstream (Fig. 3).

Fig. 3: The mechanism of zippering.

The intuition behind this zippering mechanism is a generalization of the intuition behind the WSE mechanism: if two networks fail to be linearly equivalent at an upstream stage, and their nonlinearities are necessary for the task, the disagreement will be amplified by the next nonlinear stage, and then by the next, eventually preventing the two networks from solving the same terminal task.

To justify this underlying reasoning and prove a zippering theorem, we need to upgrade from mere single-gate “usedness” (see Part 1) to layerwise minimality.

Definition (informal). A network layer is minimal if the functions in its distinct units are “identifiably separable” from each other and don’t repeat or cancel trivially. (This informal definition is made rigorous in the appendix of the Contravariance Theory paper.)

With this notion in mind, we can state a mathematically robust mechanism for the zippering phenomenon:

Zippering Theorem (informal). Let A and B be same-depth networks. Suppose they are weakly equivalent at a terminal layer s. Suppose further that at each backward step from s−1 down to q, the layers are minimal. Then, generically (that is, except on an exceptional set of network parameters of zero measure), alignment zippers upstream: for every r = q, . . . , s − 1, the layer-r representations are also weakly aligned.

The effect of the Zippering theorem is to make observations like those in Fig. 1 — and all those other ones throughout NeuroAI — a mathematical inevitability. That is, if one believes the assumptions the result needs.

Minimality avoids silly circuits . . .

Minimality is a nontrivial condition. It is possible for networks to be non-minimal, and non-minimality allows for all sorts of mischief to occur. The core problem is the theoretical possibility of null networks (see Vlačić and Bölcskei [2021] and Fefferman and Markel [1993]): networks that have multiple nontrivial layers, each of which is not itself the identity function, but whose total end-to-end effect is to compute the identity. Null networks are best thought of as “silly complex solutions to trivial problems”.

The existence of null networks would seem to impede the zippering theorem. For example, one might imagine inserting nontrivial identity blocks at different depths within a network, such that the end layer was the same for both but which as a pair clearly are not axis-aligned at each layer:

Fig. 4: A shifted identity block inserted either before or after G makes two terminally-equivalent networks (A and B) that have internally inequivalent representations. Minimality rules out silly circuits like this.

There are actually many different types of null networks2 but, as shown in the appendix of the Contravariance Theory paper, minimality either rules them out or makes them extremely unlikely.

. . . but is it biological?

Is minimality something that applies to real brains? Maybe it does: we speculate that minimality in real brains is an energetic efficiency that is evolutionarily advantageous. Perhaps the fact that model-brain similarity is actually observed empirically is as good evidence as any that the zippering theorems apply to real cases, and thus real brains are probably close to minimal. But this is far from an airtight argument.

It will be important going forward to evaluate the empirical status of minimality, or departures therefrom, both in “real world” artificial neural networks, and also in actual brains. Estimating the extent to which such systems satisfy the kind of nondegeneracy conditions needed for the zippering theorems is a crucial ingredient for creating a solid theoretical foundation for NeuroAI.

Key implication for NeuroAI: The major NeuroAI results of the past decade and a half are not accidental. Rather, modulo the biological correctness of minimality assumptions, convergent evolution between artificial networks and real brains is likely to be mathematically inevitable.

References

Thobani I, Sagastuy-Brena J, Nayebi A, Prince J, Cao R, and Yamins D (2025). Model-brain comparison using inter-animal transforms. Proceedings of the Conference on Cognitive Computational Neuroscience 2025. (Here is the original CCN version: you should read the Arxiv version but cite the CCN version.)

Yamins D and Nayebi A (2026). Contravariance Theory: Strong Alignment for Minimal Solutions to Hard Tasks. arXiv preprint arXiv:2607.08561.

Fefferman C, and Markel S (1993). Recovering a feed-forward net from its output. Advances in neural information processing systems 6.

Vlačić V, and Bölcskei H (2022). Neural network identifiability for a family of sigmoidal nonlinearities. Constructive Approximation 55, no. 1: 173-224.

1

The post-nonlinearity location is the most natural place to the make a comparison because neurons are often thought of as putting out spikes post a somatic nonlinearity.

2

In fact, if you’re curious to learn how to construct a wide variety of silly solutions to trivial problems, see Appendix A.10 of the Contravariance theory paper, which details a whole atlas of them! It also shows how the minimality conditions avoid these solutions, or makes them vanishingly rare.

items.title: The Theory of Contravariance, Part 1: Weak-Strong Equivalence (WSE)
items.description: Weak (linear) alignment and strong (axis) alignment are equivalent for hard tasks.
items.content:
(This is Part 1 of a multi-part series. See Part 0 to get the big picture.)

A big question in NeuroAI is: what is the right metric for measuring alignment of neural networks to the brain? This question has been the subject of several workshop series and multiple recent papers.

Thanks for reading The Principle Investigator! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Weak and Strong Alignment & the Strict-Loose Continuum

One overarching idea that has emerged from this literature is that some metrics are strict and some are loose. Strict metrics require very fine-grained matching between neural network parts and brain parts, while loose metrics require matching in a less constrained fashion.

The canonical example of a loose matching type is linear alignment — what we will henceforth call “weak alignment” — in which one fits a linear mapping between model feature bases and a dataset of “neuroids”.1 Linear alignment mapping is loose because it allows the source representation (the model) and the target representation (the brain) to differ up to linear reweighting of the constituent units.

For me, the purest (if not yet exactly “canonical”) example of a strict matching type is privileged axis alignment. Privileged axes are specific response functions that repeatedly arise within a model layer or brain area, across many seeds / individuals, and which are thought to capture the underlying mechanism of the computation in a finer-grained way than weak (linear span) alignment. Gabor-filter-tuned units in V1 are a canonical example of privileged axes in neuroscience (another being grid cells).

Because of this apparent deeper connection between privileged axes and mechanism, we will use the term “strong alignment” to indicate the alignment metric measuring coincidence between two networks’ privileged axes. The “strong” and “weak” terminology is also justified by the straightforward mathematical fact that strong alignment implies weak alignment — if two representations have the same privileged axes, they’ll be linearly equivalent, but not (usually) vice-versa.

There are a bunch of other metrics that people have thought about (RSA, CKA, IATC, etc) that kind of lie on a continuum along the “Strict-Loose axis”:

Weak-Strong Equivalence

It seems obvious that strong alignment is stronger than weak alignment. However, in the Contravariance Theory paper, our first main result is a proof that in an important case – namely, where two adjacent layers are weakly equivalent and where the task the network solves is suitably hard – the distinction between weak and strong alignment collapses.

Wait — we’re saying that two metrics of apparently very different strengths aren’t really that different. How can that be?

The core intuition is that if two networks are weakly aligned at layer ℓ, but have misaligned privileged axes, then after the nonlinearity at layer ℓ+1, they will be different enough that they will not even be weakly aligned there. In other words, if the two task representations are weakly related before and after a nonlinearity, the weak map must preserve the nonlinear signatures of individual coordinates. This is the essential mathematical reason that native axes can become privileged in the first place, rather than always remaining arbitrary.

This intuition relies on the nonlinearity having a nontrivial effect -- that is, it must be used:

Definition (informal): A layer-ℓ axis is used if the task and the next layer expose a genuine nonlinear effect of that axis. For ReLU, this means that the task “crosses” the zero trace set {zj = 0} and the outgoing column Wℓ+1[:, j] is nonzero.

Intuition for weak-strong equivalence: only a crossed, downstream-used zero trace set contributes a task-visible nonlinear signature. A used gate creates a slope change, and an injective affine map cannot erase that change.

The opposite of used is “degenerate” — an axis that can be removed from the nonlinear gate requirements of the network. A degenerate gate contributes nothing downstream, while a gate whose trace is not crossed is affine or zero, and can be absorbed into the adjacent affine part. The contravariance theory paper formalizes this observation via a “shrinkability lemma” in the appendix section §A.2.

The ideas of usedness and shrinkability in turn motivate a measure of task hardness in terms of how many used gates it requires. Let L be the loss function for a task. Let Fℓ,≤k be the set of networks of a fixed macroarchitecture that solve the task using at most k used layer-ℓ axes. Then define the required used-axis budget as:

The quantity mℓ(ε) is a measure of task difficulty: it counts how many nonlinear axes the task forces this layer to use.

With these ideas in mind, we can formalize the intuition described above.

Theorem (Weak-Strong Equivalence, informal): Fix adjacent layers ℓ and ℓ + 1. Suppose networks A and B are exactly weakly equivalent at both layers, and suppose the layer-ℓ axes used by the task satisfy usedness assumptions. Then every used A axis is exactly matched to a distinct B axis. Consequently, if A solves the task to loss at most ε, then

where AxisAlignℓ(A,B) is the fraction of axes alignable between networks A and B under the most axis-aligning linear map, and dℓA is the ambient dimension of network A at layer ℓ. In words: the aligned-axis fraction for adjacent weakly-aligned layers is constrained by the capacity ratio of the network (at that layer), mℓ(ε)/dℓA.

The proof of the theorem is slightly nontrivial and is given in Appendix §A.2 of the paper. But its implications are easy to understand. A network optimized to perform a task that strongly constrains it will have many or all of its gates used. Thus, the theorem says that two layers of successive weak alignment, for a sufficiently hard task, force strong privileged axis-alignment at the earlier layer.

Key implication for NeuroAI: We can interpret the Weak-Strong Equivalence (WSE) Theorem as saying, essentially: hard tasks cause privileged axes, and under the condition of a hard task, weak and strong alignment are equivalent.

A Softer WSE

The assumptions of the WSE theorem stated above are fairly strong: that two adjacent layers are exactly weakly equivalent. Of course, in the real world, we don’t usually observe exact equivalence. Instead, we observe equivalence with some measurable deficit:

The quantity ωℓ captures how weakly misaligned two networks are at layer ℓ. ωℓ = 0 means that two representations are exactly weakly aligned.

Critically, we can prove a kind of “soft” version of WSE that shows:

for some constants α and β, where AxisAlignℓθ denotes the number of axes aligned to similarity level θ. In words, if the error is already small on both sides of a nonlinear step, then many task-required gates cannot be badly misaligned, and the defect from axis alignment is an error term controlled by the two adjacent weak equivalence deficits ωℓ and ωℓ+1.

The key effect of this result is that an asymptotic equivalence applies for real-world situations. Imagine a sequence of networks An and Bn both being optimized for the same hard task. Then adjacent-layer convergence in weak-aligned representations translates into convergence in the strong axis-alignment sense:

Key implication for NeuroAI: Asymptotic weak-strong equivalence emerges: if two sequences of networks tend toward having similar representations during optimization toward a common goal, their axes eventually become aligned.

So does the choice of metric even matter?

The WSE results make one wonder: to what extent do choices of metric matter? If the two opposite ends of the Strict-Loose continuum are actually pretty equivalent in an important case, does it matter which one we choose? Our results suggest: not as much as might have been thought. This is probably why the two “main” metrics people actually use — namely, regularized linear regression and RSA — agree in a rank-order sense, to a pretty large extent, across a wide variety of models. (Note, though, that RSA is not covered by the WSE theorem, and its divergences from that framework will be a subject of a future post.)

1

A “neuroid” is whatever the unit of neural reporting a given dataset has. In an fMRI dataset this is typically a voxel. In an electrophysiology dataset, this is typically an electrode — that is, essentially, a Multi-Unit Activity (MUA) site.

items.title: The Theory of Contravariance, Part 0
items.description: Breaking down our extensive new theory paper.
items.content:
Aran Nayebi and I have just released a rather, uhm … let’s say, sizeable… new paper on the Theory of Contravariance. Because it’s a long paper and has many different ideas in it, we’re going to be writing a multi-part substack series on it, beginning with this post describing the overall purpose of the project.

What needs to be explained in NeuroAI?

Why is there apparent convergent evolution between task-driven neural network models and the brain? Over the past 15 years in NeuroAI, results in a wide variety of domains (in, e.g. vision, audition, somatosensation, navigation, motor, decision making, and human language) have found that optimizing neural networks end-to-end to solve strong cognitive-level (that is, AI-hard) tasks leads to models whose internal layers mimic the neural response properties of the brain. This happens for (i) linear span of neural responses within an area, (ii) the existence of cross-area neuroanatomical hierarchies, and (iii) even the specific privileged axes at a single-unit level. Why does all this convergent evolution happen?

Thanks for reading The Principle Investigator! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

(A) Correlations, up to linear span alignment, between performance and neural alignment of models occur across domains and modalities (each dot in each panel is a neural network model). What causes these correlations? (B) Within a model, neuroanatomically consistent hierarachies emerge. Why? (C) And, privileged axes (such as the Gabor-like structures of V1) also reliably emerge. Why? In fact, why do privileged axes exist at all?...

How does the Contravariance Principle help?

The Contravariance Principle in NeuroAI is an idea that I helped develop a few years ago while working together with the redoubtable philosopher of neuroscience, Rosa Cao (the original arXiv version appeared in 2021, but it was finally published in 2024). The contravariance principle says, basically:

Contravariance Principle (Cao & Yamins, 2021-2024): The size and dispersion of the set of (neural network) solutions to a task is contravariantly related (that is, fancy mathese for “inversely related”) to the difficulty of solving the task. The harder the task, the fewer the solutions, and the more similar they are likely to be to each other. Thus, you will be more likely to observe convergent evolution between any two solutions (be they biological or artificial) when trying to solve hard real-world tasks — even with learned solutions you don’t totally understand — rather than when completely solving toy versions of the task whose solutions you can intuitively grok.

Easy toy tasks will have many spurious solutions, and though your conceptually-clean hard-coded solution to it will totally work in the narrow case in which you conceived of it, that solution will be brittle and utterly fall apart outside that case when exposed to the complex situations of the real world.

In contrast, the somewhat hard-to-understand solution to the harder problem will be forced by the hard constraints of the task to look more like a real brain, which was evolved to deal with complex real-world circumstances in the first place.

This figure captures the concept graphically:

As you increase task constraint strength along the x-axis, the size and dispersion of the solution set to the task decreases, and the likelihood of observing “convergent evolution” between solutions increases.

Though the contravariance principle is, at least in the initial formulation of the paper with Cao, fairly mathematically obvious, it nonetheless has non-obvious consequences for neuroscience. Specifically, it has a clear prescription:

Contravariance’s Anti-Reductionist Prescription for Experimental Design: Don’t make reduced versions of your task, where you think you will be able to “completely understand” the solution mechanism. Instead, do experiments in complex situations where it’s hard to think of a hard-coded solution that will just solve the task you’re asking your animals or subjects to do. — that is to say, make experimental situations that are challenging and varied enough that the doing of the task itself is likely to be a strong constraint on the solution space. That way, your proposed theory (which will probably have to be a learned neural network) will be less likely to be spurious and more likely to be brain-like.

This prescription is rather unintuitive for many (neuro)scientists, because they are used to following the standard physics-reductionist procedure of trying to simplify the phenomenon they’re interested in down to the most reduced version that captures its essence, and then completely and totally characterizing the neural mechanism for that reduced version. The contravariance principle says that, for studying solutions to complex real-world evolutionary problems (which the brain is), the normal reductionist idea will end up being very misleading.

I think it’s fair to say that, while this realization is gaining a little bit of ground in NeuroAI, it remains mostly unaccepted by (and probably unknown to) the systems neuroscience community at large.

A Mathematical Theory of Contravariance

The original version of contravariance is pretty informal, being a primarily philosophical contribution. While that status has still supported some conceptual utility for the NeuroAI community, it has for several years been on our minds to try to see if the concept could be formalized. Given the existence of quite a bit of confusion in the field, some definitive mathematical theorems could potentially be helpful.

Visions of conjectures danced in our heads, as we tried to understand not only how to define such terms as “task difficulty”, but also to imagine what types of nontrivial and useful results could likely be derived. Recently, however, Aran and I found a route in.

The basic idea is to start with what turns out to be an easier question — namely, the relationship between linear similarity of representations at the population level, and privileged-axis alignment at the individual neuron level. As detailed in the companion post Contravariance Theory, Part 1: Weak-Strong Equivalence, it turns out that these notions are tightly bound together, in the case of hard tasks — the kind of hard tasks that contravariance asks for. In fact, we find that two apparently different metrics (“weak” linear-span equivalence and “strong” privileged-axis alignment) end up being essentially equivalent, in the hard-task limit.

The technical tools and conceptual ideas needed for Weak-Strong Equivalence (WSE) allowed us to see how to measure task difficulty. With one additional ingredient — that of minimality — we were then able to see how to extend WSE results to full contravariance: a proof that for minimal solutions to hard tasks, there are very few solutions and they are essentially all the same.

Our new arXiv paper, Contravariance Theory: Strong Alignment for Minimal Solutions to Hard Tasks, explicates the mathematical basis for these ideas. We hope you read the paper — at least the initial part, which is a gentle-ish mostly non-mathematical summary. (There is also a ~70pp. appendix with all the hairy math that you might find fun if that’s your sort of thing.)

As a guide to the new paper, in the following posts — which will appear over the next few weeks — we will discuss:

  • Weak-Strong Equivalence: how weak alignment of neural representations up to linear equivalence, in the context of hard tasks, forces strong alignment up to single-unit privileged axes. Along the way we will see how to formalize “hardness” in an appropriate way. [Posted 2026/07/13.]

  • Zippering Theorems: How weak alignment at a terminal layer, for a hard task solved with a minimal solution, can “zipper upstream” to force full contravariant similarity throughout a network hierarchy. [Posted 2/26/07/22]

  • Contravariance for Transformers: How the theory of weak-strong equivalence and zippering apply to the case of transformer architectures, explaining some interesting recent mysteries in the pattern of NeuroAI results.

  • Contravariance vs the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH): The PRH is a recent cool proposal from [Huh et al]. Our new theory sheds light on how the PRH is both related to, and quite different from, Contravariance, and maybe provides a path to PRH formalization.

  • Contravariance and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA): The new contravariance theory touches primarily on linear similarity and single-unit preferred axes. But the theory provides a framework for thinking about other metrics like RSA as well.

  • The Math Itself: A tour of the mathematical concepts behind our theory of contravariance and how they combine algebraic geometry, manifold theory, and deep learning (fairly specialist-level).

  • How we used LLMs in our research workflow. The mathematical capabilities of LLMs were an integral component of our being able to make rapid, strong progress on these problems. You might find our workflow practices helpful for your own research.

We hope you enjoy the series!

Thanks for reading The Principle Investigator! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
